cap.n0: Two qubits on a lab bench. Is that even a computer?
cap.n1: A qubit is a quantum bit,|the unit a quantum computer works with.
cap.n2: For seventeen years,|quantum computers stayed about that small:|2 qubits in 1998, 12 at most.
cap.n3: In the next nine years, one chip held over a thousand.|What changed?
cap.n4: Meet two people we made up:|an old physicist, and a young computer-science student.
cap.n5: In 1998, machines like his had two qubits:|molecules in a liquid, read by magnets.
cap.n6: They ran tiny demos,|like finding one item out of four in a single look.
cap.n7: It works. So, back to the question: is it a computer?|A gate is one basic step of a quantum program.
cap.n8: This chart is from the first lecture of Professor|Yufei Ding's course on quantum computing systems,|at UC San Diego.
cap.n10: The first stretch is the past seventeen years,|1998 to 2015.
cap.n11: The slide says 7 to 12:|those are the biggest ones,|7 qubits in 2000, then 12 in 2006.|So the red pen writes 2 to 12.
cap.n12: And under the numbers, two words: lab access.
cap.n13: For our student, that meant a locked door.|The machine lived in one lab.
cap.n14: So a computer-science student could only stand|on tiptoe and look through the glass.
cap.n15: Then, from 2016 on, the door began to give.
cap.n16: In May 2016, IBM put a five-qubit quantum|computer online for anyone to try.
cap.n17: The door was still shut, but now it had a mail slot.
cap.n18: That is cloud access:|the machine stays in the builder's lab,|and you send it a program from|your laptop over the internet.|Programs in, answers out.
cap.n20: 127 qubits in 2021.|433 in 2022, the number on her 2024 slide.
cap.n21: A year later, her slide said over a thousand.
cap.n22: To be exact:|IBM's Condor chip, December 2023, held 1,121 qubits.|The red pen fixes one digit.
cap.n23: Our physicist holds two. The student is still counting.
cap.n24: One honest catch: that 1,121-qubit|chip was a research test.
cap.n25: The machines people run code on today|have about 100 to 160 qubits,|as of October 2026.
cap.n26: More qubits only help if they make few mistakes.|After the big chip,|IBM put a smaller chip with fewer errors online.
cap.n27: And behind the door,|there was no longer one kind of machine.|There were five.
cap.n28: Superconducting circuits:|metal loops on a chip that carry|current with no resistance.
cap.n29: Ions held in a row in a vacuum.
cap.n30: Neutral atoms in a grid, chilled by lasers.
cap.n31: Photons, particles of light;|their builders say light is easier to scale.
cap.n32: And silicon spins, where each|qubit is almost a transistor,|so it can be made in chip factories.
cap.n33: Five kinds, no winner yet. The|student can't pick a stall.
cap.n34: Which raises a question:|does every quantum computer live in a freezer?
cap.n35: The superconducting ones do:|about a hundredth of a degree above absolute zero,|over 100 times colder than deep space.
cap.n36: The metal only superconducts when it is cold.|Hence the parka. And the others?
cap.n37: Ions and atoms float in a vacuum, chilled by lasers.|The box can stay at room temperature,|but some machines cool it anyway for a cleaner vacuum.
cap.n38: And light doesn't mind the heat,|but the detectors that count single|photons are kept very cold.
cap.n39: Her slide ends with one more arrow:|the future six years, to a million qubits.
cap.n40: Company roadmaps do aim at about a million.|Plans, not machines: one plans 2 million by 2030;|others give no date.
cap.n41: So here is what changed:|real machines, many kinds, all online.
cap.n42: Now they need people who write|and compile programs for them.
cap.n43: That's why the physicist is holding the door open,|and the student walks in, laptop under one arm.
cap.n44: Next time: what the field has already done.
cap.c1: quantum hardware is really developing|very fast, faster than expected
cap.c4: you can only verify the type of gates on|it, and it's not really that useful.
cap.c5: unless you are physics students and your lab|is doing quantum computing and building|quantum hardware you will never have|access to this that kind of computer
cap.c9: So generally speaking, in principle, only|superconducting requires low temperature.
cap.c10: But sometimes we still use low temperature|to get better results.
cap.c11: ion trap is a very mature technology that|has been used to build quantum computers
cap.c12: not only we have much larger quantum|computers and up to like 1,000 qubits
